# Rationale_DOC_AUDIT

Agent ID: DOC_AUDIT
Domain: Documentation + Project Reality Audit
Status: PENDING VERIFICATION

Previous rationale history is archived under `Docs/Archive/Batch004/AgentLogs/Rationale_DOC_AUDIT.md`.

## Decision 021 - PDA Must Fail Closed When The Physical Shell Is Missing

Problem: Static prefab evidence still shows `Player.prefab` `PlayerPDA` with null `pdaPanel`, null `pdaCanvasGroup`, and null tabs, while static scene/prefab scans did not prove `DiegeticPDAController` placement. Before R22, `PlayerPDA.Open()` could set `IsOpen=true`, switch to UI input, release the cursor, request PDA depth of field, play audio, and raise PDA events even if no visible PDA shell had configured the panel. That is a first-hour input trap risk.

Solution: Keep the existing diegetic bridge architecture but make the backend fail closed. R22 makes `PlayerPDA.Open()` require a renderable shell: non-null `pdaPanel` and at least one resolved tab. If the bridge has not configured the shell, open returns before mutating global PDA state or input maps. Input-map switches are also guarded against missing/uninitialized `GlobalRegistry.Input`. `ContentSanityValidator` now validates `Player.prefab` for `PlayerPDA` headless-open risk and exposes `PlayerPdaHeadlessOpenRisk` / `PlayerPdaBridgeWarnings` summary counters.

Rejected Alternatives: Creating a raw YAML PDA shell inside `Player.prefab` was rejected because hand-authoring a complex UI hierarchy without Unity import is corruption-prone and likely to fight concurrent UI agents. Adding another runtime auto-installer that instantiates UI was rejected because it would hide scene/prefab ownership instead of proving the physical shell. Leaving the issue documented only was rejected because a headless input lock is a player-facing failure mode.

Scalability potential: Low = on MX350, PDA open cannot capture controls into an invisible UI; missing shell is a clear validator/runtime error instead of a soft lock. Middle = editor validation makes prefab regressions visible before route tests. High = once the shell is mounted, richer PDA tabs can be measured without confusing backend state with presentation. Ultra = visual overkill should go into the physical tablet, phosphor/render-texture presentation, scanner visualization, and diegetic input after the shell route is proven.

Hardware Impact: Runtime guard runs only on PDA open/close input paths, not per frame; expected hot-path impact is 0 us/frame. Validator is editor-only. No Unity compile/import/PlayMode/profiler proof was run, so runtime cost remains PENDING VERIFICATION.

## Decision 022 - Duplicate Item Identity Needs An Editor Gate, Not A Runtime Guess

Problem: R21 closed the static resource-node catalog/worldPrefab route, but stable docs still correctly identified one remaining identity contamination: two `ItemData` assets share `PersistentId` / `stableId` `Data_Copper`. Static source already makes catalog ambiguity dangerous because inventory acceptance and resource pickup route through catalog hashes and runtime descriptors.

Solution: Keep runtime behavior unchanged and harden editor validation. `ContentSanityValidator` now reports duplicate `ItemData.PersistentId` across data assets, null catalog entries, duplicate catalog hashes, missing catalog runtime descriptors, and `ItemCatalog.HasLookupAmbiguity`. This catches root/raw copper-style regressions before Play Mode without adding hot-path work.

Rejected Alternatives: Deleting or renaming the legacy root copper asset was rejected without Unity/import/reference validation because historical references may still depend on its GUID. Adding a runtime disambiguation fallback was rejected because it would hide bad authored data and make save/inventory behavior less deterministic.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 route tests stop wasting time on silent hash/catalog ambiguity. Middle = content expansion gets deterministic editor failures for identity collisions. High = resource pickup presentation can improve after identity and route proof. Ultra = spend budget on scanner/PDA/mining feedback after the canonical item route is proven, not on runtime rescue logic.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validator code, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Unity MCP `validate_script` returned 0 diagnostics for `ContentSanityValidator.cs`; `dotnet build Hecton8.Editor.csproj` is still blocked by existing `Hecton8.Core` missing namespace/type errors. No Unity validator menu, Play Mode, profiler, or player build was run; runtime cost remains PENDING VERIFICATION.

## Decision 023 - Active Tool Metadata Must Prove A Player Route

Problem: Static data showed `13` active `ToolMetadata_*.asset` files but only `12` held tool prefabs and `12` tool ItemData/world-prefab routes. `ToolMetadata_LogicSpanner.asset` plus `LogicSpannerTool.cs` is real authored work, but it has no `Item_Tool_LogicSpanner.asset`, held prefab, world prefab, catalog ref, recipe ref, or loadout route. That is not a build bug; it is partial gameplay content sitting in active data where future reports can mistake it for player-available functionality.

Solution: Keep runtime untouched and extend the editor content gate. R24 makes `ContentSanityValidator` scan held tool prefabs under `Assets/_Project/Prefabs/Tools/Held`, validate `PlayerTool.Metadata`, `PlayerTool.ToolData`, `ItemCategory.Tool`, `ItemCatalog` runtime descriptor, and non-null tool `worldPrefab`. It also validates active `ToolMetadata` assets for empty/duplicate `toolID` and reports metadata with no held prefab route as orphan gameplay content. Static expectation: `ToolMetadataOrphans=1` for `ToolMetadata_LogicSpanner.asset` until the full route is authored or the metadata is quarantined outside active data.

Rejected Alternatives: Creating `Item_Tool_LogicSpanner.asset` / prefabs by hand was rejected because that would require Unity import, GUID-safe prefab authoring, icon/world pickup presentation, recipe economy, and acquisition balance proof under a loaded machine. Leaving the finding in docs only was rejected because the same orphan route can recur as more tools are added. Adding runtime fallback grants was rejected because it would hide authored-data incompleteness and contaminate first-hour route proof.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 builds do not carry fake player-available tools in active validation reports; route failures are editor errors before runtime. Middle = content expansion gets a deterministic gate for tool acquisition/equip/drop routes. High = tool visuals can scale after each tool has a real route. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in held/world/pickup presentation and PDA loadout feedback after the canonical route exists, not in metadata-only content.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validation, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Static readback and `git diff --check` were used; no Unity validator menu, import, Play Mode, profiler, dotnet build, or runtime tool-route proof was run due machine-load constraint.

## Decision 024 - Dev Provisioning Must Not Re-enter The First-Hour Path Silently

Problem: R18 disabled `ToolLoadoutProvisioner` startup grants on `Player.prefab`, but the component remains serialized on the canonical player with direct tool/material references. Static YAML currently shows the dangerous flags off, yet without an editor gate a later prefab edit can re-enable hidden inventory/loadout/construction-material grants and poison first-hour route proof again.

Solution: Keep the dev helper for explicit editor/development validation, but make accidental startup grants a content-validation failure. R25 extends `ContentSanityValidator` to load `Player.prefab`, find `ToolLoadoutProvisioner`, and report `PlayerDevProvisionerStartupRisk` if `provisionInventoryOnStart`, `assignCoreLoadoutOnStart`, or `provisionConstructionMaterialsOnStart` is true on the canonical player prefab.

Rejected Alternatives: Removing the component by raw prefab YAML was rejected because it can fight concurrent agents and lose explicit editor/development validation affordances. Relying on the existing `UNITY_EDITOR || DEVELOPMENT_BUILD` runtime guard was rejected because it does not protect Play Mode/dev proof from false positives. Leaving the R18 finding documented only was rejected because hidden grants are exactly the kind of regression docs fail to prevent.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 first-hour smoke runs stop accepting artificial startup grants as progress. Middle = route tests can distinguish real acquisition from dev fixtures. High = richer tool loadout UX can be validated after acquisition truth is stable. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in crafted/equipped/physical tool presentation after the clean route exists.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validation, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Static prefab/source readback and `git diff --check` were used; no Unity menu, import, Play Mode, profiler, dotnet build, or runtime route proof was run.

## Decision 025 - Quest Strings Need Catalog/Graph Validation

Problem: `QuestData` uses string IDs for item/craft triggers, completion items, critical item rollback, and prerequisite quest IDs. The runtime quest graph is packed/native and serious, but missing or stale authoring strings would compile into dead quest nodes or impossible first-hour progression. Current static first-hour strings resolve: `Data_TitaniumScrap`, `Item_Tool_Scanner`, and cataloged raw `Data_Copper` exist in `ItemCatalog`, and checked first-hour prerequisites point to existing quest IDs. The risk is recurrence as content expands.

Solution: Extend `ContentSanityValidator` with an editor-only quest route gate. R26 validates `QuestData.questId` non-empty/unique, `prerequisiteQuestIds` against the active quest set, `OnItemCollected` / `OnCraftCompleted` trigger and completion IDs against `ItemCatalog` runtime descriptors, and non-empty `criticalItemId` against the same catalog route. The validator summary now reports `Quests` and `QuestRouteErrors`.

Rejected Alternatives: Hardcoding first-hour quest IDs in runtime was rejected because it couples content to code and does not scale. Trusting `QuestStateManager` compile diagnostics alone was rejected because it catches graph hash issues but not authored item IDs missing from the catalog. Editing quest assets by hand was rejected because current static evidence does not show an actual broken quest string.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 first-hour route tests fail early when a quest points at a missing item instead of wasting runtime passes. Middle = authored quest expansion gets deterministic item/prerequisite validation. High = richer PDA/quest presentation can scale after the graph is data-clean. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in quest presentation, scanner feedback, and physical PDA after route truth is stable.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validation, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Static item/catalog/prerequisite scans and `git diff --check` were used; no Unity validator menu, import, Play Mode, profiler, dotnet build, pickup/craft route, or save/load proof was run.

## Decision 026 - Craft Quests Need Recipe-Result Proof, Not Just Catalog IDs

Problem: R26 proved quest item strings against the catalog, but that is not enough for `OnCraftCompleted`. A quest can point to `Item_Tool_Scanner` and still be impossible if no valid `RecipeData` crafts that item, or if the recipe has null result, empty ingredients, bad quantities, missing fabrication group, or ingredient refs outside `ItemCatalog`. Static filesystem evidence found `41` authored recipe assets and `Recipe_Scanner.asset` outputs `Item_Tool_Scanner`, but there was no general editor gate preventing craft-route regressions.

Solution: Add an editor-only recipe validation pass to `ContentSanityValidator`. R27 validates `RecipeData` runtime hash uniqueness, result item catalog descriptor, positive result quantity, explicit fabrication group, non-empty ingredient list, positive ingredient amounts, and ingredient catalog descriptors. The pass returns valid recipe result persistent IDs, and `QuestData.OnCraftCompleted` trigger/completion IDs are cross-checked against that set. The validator summary now reports `Recipes` and `RecipeRouteErrors`.

Rejected Alternatives: Running Play Mode fabricator proof was rejected due the active machine-load constraint. Hand-editing recipe YAML was rejected because current static evidence shows no specific broken scanner recipe field. Trusting `Fabricator.CanCraft` runtime rejection was rejected because it fails too late and can make first-hour progression look like a quest/runtime bug when the real issue is bad authored data.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 first-hour craft tests fail at content validation when a recipe route is missing instead of burning runtime passes. Middle = recipe expansion gets deterministic catalog/ingredient/category gates. High = PDA/fabricator presentation can scale after recipe data is route-clean. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in fabrication animation, diegetic screens, tool reveal, and scanner feedback after recipe-result truth is stable.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validation, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Static readback, recipe asset count, `Recipe_Scanner.asset` YAML check, and `git diff --check` were used; no Unity menu, import, Play Mode, profiler, dotnet build, fabricator UI route, or save/load proof was run.

## Decision 027 - Scan-Locked Recipes Need Unlock Route Warnings

Problem: R27 validated recipe structure and craft-quest recipe outputs, but scan-locked recipes can still be unreachable. Static search found `scan.resource_node` has a visible runtime/generic route in `ScanLogSystem` / `ScannerTool`, while `scan.expedition_contact`, `scan.resource_cache`, and `scan.structure_relay` currently appear only in recipe assets and editor authoring scripts. `ConstructionBootstrapAuthoring` can create scannable probes with those IDs, but source authoring capability is not proof that production scene/prefab content contains those probes or that a player can unlock them before the recipe is needed.

Solution: Add a warning-level scan-gate route check to `ContentSanityValidator`. R28 collects known generic scan IDs and authored `ScannableTarget` prefab entry IDs under `Assets/_Project/Prefabs`, then warns when `RecipeData.requiredScanEntryId` has no known route. The summary now reports `RecipeScanGateWarnings`. This is intentionally not a hard error because some routes may be produced by an explicit editor bootstrap scene, but it blocks false confidence in first-hour craft readiness.

Rejected Alternatives: Making all unknown scan gates hard errors was rejected because it can false-fail generated proving-ground content. Removing scan locks from scanner/analyzer recipes by raw YAML was rejected because that changes progression/economy without runtime design proof. Ignoring scan locks was rejected because a clean recipe result route is not enough if the recipe never appears.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 first-hour tests stop wasting passes on invisible recipe locks. Middle = recipe expansion gets a cheap authored-unlock warning before QA. High = scanner/fabricator/PDA UX can scale after unlock routes are explicit. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in scan discovery, probe presentation, and recipe reveal once unlock route truth is proven.

Hardware Impact: Editor-only validation, 0 us/frame runtime impact. Static grep showed the scan IDs are currently data/editor-authoring visible; `git diff --check` reported only CRLF warnings. No Unity menu, import, Play Mode, profiler, dotnet build, scan interaction, recipe unlock, fabricator UI route, or save/load proof was run.

## Decision 028 - World Pager Must Fail Closed When The Page File Is Locked

Problem: Fresh Unity Console evidence after compile reconciliation no longer showed C# compiler errors, but it did show a bootstrap/runtime fault: `H8BinaryWorldPager` threw `IOException: Sharing violation on path ... world_data.h8bin`, which propagated through `SaveManager` and failed `GameBootstrapper` CoreServices with `BIOS ERROR 0xBOOT_TIMEOUT`. In a multi-editor/parallel-agent workspace, one locked persistence page file must not prevent the project from bootstrapping.

Solution: Keep the async pager and fixed-size native queues, but make initialization fail closed on file-system ownership failures. `H8BinaryWorldPager.Initialize()` now catches `IOException` and `UnauthorizedAccessException`, records an initialization fault, increments IO telemetry, emits one development warning, and leaves the pager uninitialized so write/read calls reject rather than throwing. `SaveManager` now checks `HasInitializationFault` before retrying initialization, preventing per-frame open spam. During the same pass, duplicate `SaveManager` dehydration-drain/notification methods were collapsed to the bounded route that writes voxel, inventory, and metadata payloads, and public pager APIs were returned to safe C# signatures so normal services can call them without unsafe context leakage.

Rejected Alternatives: Switching the page file to `FileShare.ReadWrite` was rejected because it hides multi-writer corruption risk. Killing the other Unity/editor process was rejected as an environmental workaround, not a product fix. Retrying the open every tick was rejected because a locked file would turn persistence into repeated IO exceptions/log spam. Treating the fault as fatal was rejected because persistence degradation is preferable to blocking bootstrap in editor/development environments.

Scalability potential: Low = on MX350 or parallel-editor machines, the game can still bootstrap when async page persistence is temporarily unavailable; chunk page IO rejects cleanly instead of stalling the boot route. Middle = save/load proof can now distinguish persistence-backend availability from global bootstrap health. High = the world pager can keep its bounded native queues and background worker when the file is available. Ultra = visual/system overkill should be bought after persistence has explicit save/load/profiler proof, not by allowing a locked disk file to take down the world.

Hardware Impact: Hot-path impact after a lock fault is 0 us/frame for open retries because `SaveManager` does not reinitialize a faulted pager. Normal initialized pager behavior remains fixed-queue/background IO; no PlayMode/profiler/GC proof was captured. Unity `6000.4.1f1` batchmode import/script compilation ran with `Library/Codex_DOC_AUDIT_UnityBatchCompile.log`; strict scan found no `error CS`, bootstrap exception, or BIOS timeout lines, and the log ended `Exiting batchmode successfully`. A later read-only Unity MCP Console readback first returned `0` errors and `7` warnings from ADB/Crest/MCP bridge/serializer surfaces; final read-only Console readback returned `0` log entries. Runtime save/load correctness remains PENDING VERIFICATION.

## Decision 029 - Async Pager Compile Clean Is Not Chunk Persistence Correctness

Problem: R29 fixed the visible compile/bootstrap layer, but static source review found deeper pager correctness issues. `H8BinaryWorldPager` still opened `world_data.h8bin` with `FileShare.ReadWrite`, directly contradicting the single-writer corruption boundary recorded in Decision 028. The pager worker needed a bounded stop handshake before native disposal; otherwise `Dispose()` could release native arenas while the worker was still alive. `TryCopyCompletedPage()` could leave ready results pinned when the destination/result was invalid. Unwritten sparse sectors and hash-collided pages were classified as corruption, causing false black-box dumps. At the integration layer, `SaveManager.EnqueueChunkDehydrationPayloads()` captured the entire global `VoxelDeltaProcessor` native snapshot for every dehydrated chunk, then wrote it as a chunk page; `WorldChunkResidencyManager` requested voxel page reads without an apply route, so ready payloads were telemetry at best, not hydration.

Solution: R30 corrected the pager from "compile-clean experimental route" toward fail-closed correctness. `world_data.h8bin` now uses `FileShare.Read`, preserving diagnostic readers while rejecting concurrent writers. The pager worker now uses `_workerStopLock`, `Monitor.Wait`, and `Monitor.PulseAll` to bound shutdown before native disposal. Invalid ready read results now release their slot/result instead of poisoning the fixed read ring. Empty headers and valid headers for a different sector/payload resolve as `Missing`, not `Corrupt`, because sparse random-access files and fixed-slot hash collisions are fallback cases, not evidence of disk corruption. `SaveManager` no longer writes global voxel snapshots on chunk dehydration; it keeps only inventory-shadow and chunk metadata sidecar writes until a real chunk-local voxel snapshot/apply contract exists. `WorldChunkResidencyManager.RequestLoad()` no longer enqueues orphaned `VoxelDeltaRle` prefetch requests.

Rejected Alternatives: Keeping `FileShare.ReadWrite` was rejected because it permits two writers to silently corrupt the same fixed-slot binary sidecar. Applying pager-ready voxel payloads inside `WorldChunkResidencyManager` was rejected because the payload currently represents a global `VoxelDeltaProcessor` snapshot, not an isolated chunk-local delta; applying it during chunk hydrate could overwrite unrelated voxel state. Writing a chunk-specific capture by guessing from `chunkId` was rejected because `VoxelDeltaProcessor.ChunkAddress` uses chunk coord and voxel size, while the streaming chunk id is AUP-derived; inventing that mapping in persistence would create another hidden cross-domain dependency. Leaving the R29 route untouched was rejected because it would turn compile success into false persistence confidence.

Scalability potential: Low = on MX350, chunk unload no longer performs a potentially large global voxel snapshot allocation/write per dehydrated chunk, and unwritten sparse pages fall back without corruption spam. Middle = page IO now has single-writer semantics and bounded result cleanup, making later save/load proof less noisy. High = a future chunk-local voxel delta contract can reuse the pager API once capture/apply semantics are real. Ultra = visual/system overkill should be bought after chunk persistence is artifact-proven; until then, saved cycles belong to stable streaming, impostors, and visible feedback, not fake hydrate telemetry.

Hardware Impact: Hot path impact is expected to improve under streaming churn because R30 removes one potentially large `Allocator.Persistent` voxel snapshot capture and 256 KB page write attempt per dehydrated chunk. Pager open/write/read hot paths remain fixed-queue/native-copy based. Shutdown cost can add up to `250 ms` bounded wait only during controlled disposal, not per frame. No Unity import, PlayMode, save/load roundtrip, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R30, so the performance numbers remain engineering estimates, not measured proof.

## Decision 030 - Pager Sidecar Must Not Be A Boot Dependency Without Runtime Proof

Problem: After R30, concurrent workspace churn reintroduced the exact bad chunk-dehydration path: `SaveManager.EnqueueChunkDehydrationPayloads()` again captured a full global `VoxelDeltaProcessor` native snapshot and labeled it `worldPagerVoxelDeltaSnapshot`. Static source also showed `InitializeNativeBuffers()` opening `world_data.h8bin` during `SaveManager.Awake()` / `InitializeService()`. That made the async sidecar pager a cold-boot dependency even when no chunk page IO had been requested, while the remaining 132 MB save-buffer residency is still unproven on low-end hardware.

Solution: R31 removes the returned global voxel snapshot block again and keeps sidecar chunk dehydration limited to inventory shadow plus chunk metadata. `InitializeNativeBuffers()` no longer calls `EnsureWorldPagerInitialized()`, so the binary pager object/file/native queues are created only when an actual chunk sidecar write/read path asks for them. The main save/load native buffers are left unchanged because lazy-loading those arenas is a larger behavioral refactor and needs PlayMode/save-load proof.

Rejected Alternatives: Full lazy allocation of the 64 MB raw save buffer and 68 MB compressed buffer was rejected in this pass because it touches core save/load timing and failure behavior without runtime proof. Guessing a chunk-local voxel mapping was rejected again because the current available snapshot is global, not a safe per-chunk payload. Running Unity, dotnet, PlayMode, profiler, or Memory Profiler was rejected under the user's machine-load constraint.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350/editor boot no longer pays a pager file-open/native-pager cost before sidecar IO is needed, and chunk unload does not serialize a global voxel blob. Middle = persistence proof can measure save-buffer residency separately from pager sidecar residency. High = chunk-local page IO can be reintroduced when capture/apply ownership is explicit. Ultra = visual overkill should be bought by stable streaming and visible feedback after persistence artifacts prove the sidecar route, not by boot-opening unused binary files.

Hardware Impact: Expected cold-boot improvement is removal of one `world_data.h8bin` open attempt plus `H8BinaryWorldPager` object/native queue/arena residency until first sidecar IO. Expected streaming improvement is again removal of one potentially large native snapshot allocation and 256 KB page-write attempt per dehydrated chunk. No Unity import, PlayMode, save/load roundtrip, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R31, so these remain engineering estimates.

## Decision 031 - Save Buffers Belong To First Persistence Use, Not Boot

Problem: R31 removed the pager file-open dependency from boot, but `SaveManager.Awake()` / `InitializeService()` still called `InitializeNativeBuffers()` and allocated the large save working set immediately: 64 MB raw payload buffer, about 68 MB compressed payload buffer, and 10 MB staging arena. That is defensible for an instant-save product only after memory evidence. Without Memory Profiler proof it is a hard low-tier boot tax.

Solution: R32 splits always-on state from working persistence buffers. Boot now initializes only the `300`-entry save telemetry ring and the `9`-entry load-candidate scratch. The raw payload, compressed payload, and staging arenas are allocated on first actual persistence use: full save gets `EnsureSaveWorkingBuffers()`, load gets the raw buffer plus candidate scratch before `_isBusy` is set, and chunk sidecar dehydration gets only the 10 MB staging arena. This preserves existing binary format and save/load pipeline ownership while removing large cold-boot residency.

Rejected Alternatives: Shrinking the save payload capacity was rejected because it changes save-format limits and needs data-size proof. Disposing the large buffers immediately after every save/load was rejected for now because repeated allocation/free during autosave churn can create stalls; persistent-after-first-use is the conservative middle step. Leaving all buffers at boot was rejected because it makes low-end boot pay for a feature that may not run during the first minutes of play.

Scalability potential: Low = toaster/MX350 boot no longer reserves the large save working set before first persistence operation. Middle = first save/load still pays a visible cold allocation burst, which can be scheduled behind UI/loading if needed. High = later Memory Profiler proof can decide whether to release buffers after use, pool them, or keep them resident for instant autosave. Ultra = high-end devices can keep resident persistence arenas after first use and spend saved boot budget on richer streaming/feedback instead of invisible preallocation.

Hardware Impact: Expected cold-boot native residency reduction is approximately 64 MB + 68 MB + 10 MB, minus tiny telemetry/candidate scratch retained at boot. First save/load/chunk-sidecar use now pays the allocation cost explicitly. No Unity import, PlayMode, save/load roundtrip, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R32, so this is static engineering evidence, not measured proof.

## Decision 032 - Lazy Allocation Must Fail Closed Before It Allocates

Problem: R32 moved large save buffers to first use, but the first-use boundaries still had two weak edges. Chunk dehydration called `EnsureWorldPagerInitialized()` and then allocated the 10 MB staging arena if `_worldPager` was merely non-null; a locked or faulted pager would reject writes anyway, so that fault path could still pay staging memory. `LoadGameAsync()` allocated the raw buffer and load-candidate scratch before entering the `try/finally`, so a NativeArray allocation failure could bypass the normal load failure reporting and `_isBusy` cleanup envelope.

Solution: R33 makes the chunk sidecar path return unless the pager exists, is initialized, and has no initialization fault before allocating `_saveStagingBuffer`. Load first-use allocation now happens inside the load `try` with `candidates` initialized to default; `ClearLoadCandidates()` already handles default/uncreated arrays safely. This keeps the lazy allocation policy but removes avoidable fault-path residency and routes allocation failure through the same load failure path as IO/format errors.

Rejected Alternatives: Allocating staging before pager readiness was rejected because it spends memory on a write path known to reject. Leaving load allocation before the `try` was rejected because low-memory failures should not skip user-visible failure state. Catching allocation separately was rejected because the existing load error envelope already records failure, raises events, hides the loading screen, and clears busy state.

Scalability potential: Low = on MX350/parallel-editor machines, a locked `world_data.h8bin` no longer triggers 10 MB staging allocation through chunk dehydration. Middle = low-memory load failures have one consistent failure path. High = later profiler proof can evaluate whether staging should release after sidecar churn. Ultra = high-end devices can still keep first-use buffers resident after successful use, but fault paths stay cheap and deterministic.

Hardware Impact: Expected fault-path native residency reduction is 10 MB when the pager cannot initialize. Load allocation failure now uses the managed failure path instead of escaping before cleanup. No Unity import, PlayMode, save/load roundtrip, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R33.

## Decision 033 - HectonPlayerMovement Is Load-Bearing, But Hot Lookup Debt Still Gets Cut

Problem: `HectonPlayerMovement.cs` is currently 740,426 bytes / 13,240 lines. It is not "walking code"; it is a fused integration hub for locomotion, KCC, water state, transport, hazards, camera/presentation, AUP repair, probes, and telemetry. A blind split would be high regression risk. However, static hot-path review found ladder spline snap resolving `ClimbableLadder` from the collider via `TryGetComponent` in the fixed locomotion ladder-probe path. That is small but real hot-path lookup debt.

Solution: Keep the owner intact and add a narrow positive cache: `_cachedLadderSnapColliderInstanceId` plus `_cachedLadderSnapComponent`. `TryResolveLadderSnapFrame` is now instance-owned, reuses the cached ladder for the same collider, and clears stale cache if resolution fails. Behavior stays the same; the change only avoids repeated collider component resolution on continued ladder contact.

Rejected Alternatives: Splitting `HectonPlayerMovement` was rejected because the file is load-bearing and lacks a fresh PlayMode/profiler baseline. Replacing the ladder probe with a new async query contract was rejected because the existing motor already provides recent batched ladder hits. Caching negative misses permanently was rejected because dynamic scene edits/prefab changes could add a ladder component later; the cache stores only positive component resolution.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 fixed locomotion path avoids repeated component lookup while ladder snap is active. Middle = future player-controller decomposition should start from seams with existing caches/probes, not broad rewrites. High = profiler proof can decide whether footstep material parent-provider lookup, hazard influence, and presentation signals need similar caching or extraction. Ultra = visual overkill belongs in presentation layers after fixed locomotion remains deterministic and cheap.

Hardware Impact: Expected cost reduction is small and localized: one repeated collider component lookup avoided during ladder snap reuse. No Unity import, PlayMode, ladder interaction proof, profiler, GCMonitor, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R34.

## Decision 034 - PDA HLOD Points Need Dirty-Version Uploads, Not Repeated Fixed Buffer Writes

Problem: The `WORLD_STREAMING_LOD_MANAGER` reports correctly moved HLOD impostor residency toward native SOA and GPU-resident matrix streams, but static source review found `PDAMapTab.TryResolveHlodImpostorAupBuffer()` still uploaded its fixed `16`-point HLOD AUP buffer every map build whenever at least one impostor point existed. That is bounded, but it violates the bandwidth discipline rule: unchanged data must not be resent just because a consumer rendered another pass.

Solution: Expand `IStreamingBackpressureService` with scalar `ActiveImpostorVersion` and implement it as a separate point/read-model version in `WorldChunkResidencyManager`. `PDAMapTab` now caches uploaded HLOD version/count, clamps count to the native point array length, clears unused fixed slots only when the read model changes, and skips `GraphicsBufferUploadUtility.UploadArray` on unchanged HLOD point data. Renderer matrix dirty state remains separate from PDA point dirty state, so fade-progress point updates can advance the PDA version without forcing renderer matrix uploads.

Rejected Alternatives: Reusing `_activeImpostorVersion` directly was rejected because it is already the renderer matrix version; advancing it for PDA fade progress would reintroduce matrix uploads during transitions. Ignoring PDA `Fade01` changes was rejected because the map overlay would display stale fade state. Adding a new concrete PDA-to-world dependency was rejected because the existing `IStreamingBackpressureService` boundary is the correct read model.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 avoids repeated unchanged fixed HLOD POI uploads while the PDA map is open. Middle = transient fade updates still publish bounded 16-point changes. High = longer HLOD range can feed PDA without increasing CPU object churn. Ultra = saved bandwidth can be spent on richer cartography/sonar presentation after runtime proof, not on resending identical overlay data.

Hardware Impact: Expected saving is one skipped `16 x float4` PDA HLOD buffer upload per unchanged map build with active distant impostors. Fade-out transitions still upload while `Fade01` changes. No Unity import, PlayMode, PDA map proof, profiler, GCMonitor, Frame Debugger, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R35.

## Decision 035 - Recurrent Chunk Pager Voxel Writes Are A Regression, Not A Feature

Problem: Final regression grep after R35 found `worldPagerVoxelDeltaSnapshot` reintroduced in `SaveManager.EnqueueChunkDehydrationPayloads()`. That block captured the entire global `VoxelDeltaProcessor` snapshot for every dehydrated chunk and wrote it as `H8WorldPagePayloadTypes.VoxelDeltaRle`. This is the same correctness problem documented in Decisions 029 and 030: the payload is global, not chunk-local, and chunk hydration still has no safe apply contract.

Solution: Remove the recurrent block again. Chunk dehydration sidecar writes are limited to inventory shadow and `ChunkDehydratedSignal` metadata until a real chunk-local voxel delta capture/apply contract exists. The post-fix scoped grep found no `FileShare.ReadWrite`, no `worldPagerVoxelDeltaSnapshot`, and no direct `RequestAsyncPagerRead(chunkId)` in the pager integration files.

Rejected Alternatives: Keeping the write as harmless telemetry was rejected because it consumes native memory and page IO under a false chunk-local label. Applying the global snapshot during chunk hydrate was rejected because it can overwrite unrelated voxel state. Guessing a chunk-local mapping from the current chunk id was rejected because the existing snapshot API is not scoped that way.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 streaming no longer pays a potentially large global snapshot allocation/write for each dehydrated chunk. Middle = persistence proof can focus on inventory/metadata sidecars without fake voxel success. High = a chunk-local voxel contract can be added later with explicit ownership. Ultra = saved IO/memory budget belongs to visible streaming/HLOD feedback after correctness proof, not false persistence payloads.

Hardware Impact: Expected saving is the removal of one global native voxel snapshot capture and one `VoxelDeltaRle` page write attempt per dehydrated chunk. No Unity import, PlayMode, save/load roundtrip, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, or frame-time measurement was run in R36.

## Decision 036 - Compile Evidence Must Follow The Latest Concurrent Source Snapshot

Problem: After the R36 voxel-snapshot regression guard, concurrent churn reintroduced `async void RunWorkerAsync()` / `Awaitable.BackgroundThreadAsync()` inside `H8BinaryWorldPager`. The same reconciliation pass exposed `Hecton8.Core.Memory` compile walls when `GlobalDataVault` referenced Burst/Mathematics/GlobalSignals surfaces that are not available through its Bee response-file boundary. Reporting R36 as final would have been stale.

Solution: Restore `H8BinaryWorldPager` to an explicitly owned background `Thread` with `_workerThread`, `RunWorkerLoop()`, and a `Join()`-first shutdown wait before the existing monitor fallback. Keep `GlobalDataVault` inside the `Hecton8.Core.Memory` asmdef boundary: no Burst attribute, no Unity.Mathematics rcp dependency, no `GlobalSignals`/`MemoryAddressShiftSignal` dependency. Validate with Unity Bee/Roslyn response files, using temp output/refout paths: `Hecton8.Core.Memory` exit code `0`, then `Hecton8.Core` exit code `0` with the temp Core.Memory ref.

Rejected Alternatives: Trusting the earlier successful compile was rejected because the source changed after it. Keeping `Awaitable.BackgroundThreadAsync` was rejected because the pager needs a joinable worker before native arena disposal. Adding Burst/Mathematics/Core references to `Hecton8.Core.Memory.asmdef` was rejected because it expands the lowest memory layer to satisfy a local audit helper. Claiming Unity clean was rejected because Unity MCP Console returned `no_unity_session`.

Scalability potential: Low = MX350 editor/runtime paths keep pager shutdown deterministic and avoid hidden native arena races. Middle = Core.Memory remains a small dependency island that other asmdefs can reference without pulling extra signal/math packages. High = persistence and memory audits can be measured once Unity import/PlayMode is stable. Ultra = saved engineering risk should be spent on real chunk-local persistence and visible streaming feedback after runtime proof, not on false async/background ownership.

Hardware Impact: Runtime hot-path saving is not measured. Expected risk reduction is shutdown/cold-path correctness: one joinable pager worker instead of fire-and-forget async, plus no Core.Memory dependency expansion. Local compile evidence exists; Unity import, PlayMode, profiler, GCMonitor, Memory Profiler, player build, save/load roundtrip, and frame-time measurement remain PENDING VERIFICATION.

Problem: SlowTick clumping must be fixed without inventing direct dependencies across parallel agent work.
Solution: Use the extracted XML prompt, AGENTS.md, domain map, and task-relevant mandates as the only authority before code changes.
Rejected Alternatives: Directly editing suspected SlowTick code without registry/dispatcher audit was rejected because it would risk API invention and hidden dependencies.
Scalability potential: Low uses wider buckets and flat CPU load; Middle keeps stable cadence; High/Ultra can spend saved CPU on denser visual systems while preserving deterministic authority.
Hardware Impact: Expected gain on i3/MX350 is spike flattening, not total work elimination. Exact microseconds saved are PENDING PROFILER.

## Decision 1: Use Core Interface Boundary
Problem: A bucketer touches AI, voxel, thermodynamics, and dispatcher code. Direct concrete references would couple parallel agents.
Solution: Prefer an `ISimulationBucketer` service registered through `GlobalRegistry` and consumed through stable contract calls outside hot dependency lookup paths.
Rejected Alternatives: `BucketManager.Instance` and direct class references were rejected because AGENTS.md forbids singleton access and cross-domain concrete coupling.
Scalability potential: Low/MX350 can stretch cadence to reduce spikes; Ultra can process richer non-authoritative visual workload after authority buckets stay flat.
Hardware Impact: Avoids per-frame global searches and removes synchronous clump spikes. Exact microseconds saved are PENDING PROFILER.

## Decision 2: Round Cadence Domains To Power-Of-Two Masks
Problem: The assignment requested slow=60/cold=600, but the recursive verification protocol explicitly rejects hot modulo/division in Burst-visible bucket math.
Solution: Use fast=4, standard slow=64, low slow=128, cold=512. All active bucket checks resolve through `& (PowerOfTwo - 1)`.
Rejected Alternatives: `% 60`, `% 120`, `% 600`, and a mixed exact-count + division path were rejected because they create slower hot math and more branch cases.
Scalability potential: Low uses 128 buckets for toaster-grade flattening; Middle/High use 64 with optional two active buckets; Ultra spends the stable budget on visual overkill instead of authority spikes.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 5-25 us saved per broad bucket evaluation pass and larger indirect savings from flattened slow-tick bursts. Exact profiler capture is blocked by external compile errors.

## Decision 3: Bootstrap-Owned Persistent NativeArray Registry
Problem: Entity-to-bucket assignment needs stable storage without managed allocation churn and without inventing a singleton.
Solution: `GameBootstrapper` creates `ModuloSimulationBucketer` once, the service allocates persistent `NativeArray<int>` through `H8Memory`, and shutdown unregisters/disposes it.
Rejected Alternatives: `Dictionary<uint,int>`, per-system arrays, or transient frame allocations were rejected because they violate Zero-GC and cross-domain ownership rules.
Scalability potential: Low can keep a smaller active slice while preserving the same entity table; High/Ultra can raise visual workload without changing the authority contract.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 60-250 us saved under fauna-scale lookup pressure versus managed table churn; no per-frame GC allocation introduced.

## Decision 4: Dispatcher Is The Only Frame Authority
Problem: Local per-system timers caused all slow systems to wake on the same cadence, creating a spike every sixth frame on 60fps targets.
Solution: Advance the bucketer in `SystemDispatcher.Update()` after time state refresh and before simulation lanes. Dispatcher gates `IBucketedSlowTickable` objects and reports bucket load telemetry.
Rejected Alternatives: Local counters inside fauna, voxel, and thermal systems were rejected because independent timers drift and still clump after scene transitions.
Scalability potential: Low reduces active slow buckets; High can process two slow buckets per frame when debt is absent; Ultra keeps authority flat and buys stronger presentation systems.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 300-1500 us spike flattening at 5000 fauna, plus 200-900 us deferred under job-admission debt. Exact numbers require profiler after the compile wall clears.

## Decision 5: AUP Barrier Uses Cadence Throttle, Not Special Physics
Problem: Bucketing is frame-based while AUP/floating-origin shifts are spatial; staggered interpolation can tear during origin-shift locks.
Solution: Treat active AUP locks as a bucketer barrier, force one active slow bucket, and replace frame-count modulo watchdogs with countdown state.
Rejected Alternatives: Recomputing all staggered entities on an AUP frame was rejected because it recreates the exact spike the bucketer removes.
Scalability potential: Low devices get minimal authority work during shifts; Ultra can layer visual smoothing while authority remains single-bucket deterministic.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 50-200 us spike flattening during shift/watchdog frames and lower visible tear risk.

## Decision 6: Voxel And Biolum Use Fast Bucket Fakes
Problem: Queue drains and distant biolum LOD checks can clump when driven from raw frame modulo checks.
Solution: Hash carve events/zones into the 4-bucket fast domain and only process matching active fast buckets. This is a scheduling fake, not a physics simulation.
Rejected Alternatives: Full queue drain and `Time.frameCount % 3` LOD gating were rejected because they synchronize unrelated work on the same frame.
Scalability potential: Low spreads expensive world edits across frames; High/Ultra can spend the saved frame budget on richer particle/light response.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 100-600 us spike flattening during voxel carve bursts and 25-90 us around distant biolum update bursts.

## Decision 7: Thermodynamics Uses 1/8 Slice Instead Of Exact 1/6
Problem: The prompt asked for 1/6 Jacobi diffusion, but the same prompt requires replacing modulo with power-of-two masks after core completion.
Solution: Slice the 32^3 thermal grid into 8 equal chunks, schedule one slice per job, and use shift/mask coordinate decode in the owned Jacobi job.
Rejected Alternatives: Exact 1/6 slicing and `% Width`/`% Depth` decode were rejected because they put division/modulo back into a Burst job.
Scalability potential: Low amortizes diffusion across more frames with stable visuals; Ultra can increase visual projection quality because the authority heat grid no longer clumps.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 500-1800 us spike flattening during thermal diffusion sweeps; total work remains similar, frame pacing improves.

## Decision 8: Stop At First External Compile Wall
Problem: The first Unity compile failed in `DeployableSdfDrillRuntime`, a mining-domain file that did not implement unrelated interfaces.
Solution: Mark Task 18 as `[BLOCKED BY DEPENDENCY]`, record the exact files/errors, and avoid editing another agent's domain.
Rejected Alternatives: Patching mining runtime interfaces from this bucketer task was rejected as cross-domain sabotage risk.
Scalability potential: Bucketer code remains isolated and ready for verification after the external compile wall clears.
Hardware Impact: No runtime impact; verification is blocked, not implementation.

## Decision 9: Prevent High-Tier Bucket Overlap
Problem: A two-active-bucket high-tier mode can silently double-sample entities if it slides a `{active, active+1}` window every frame.
Solution: Convert active slow buckets into non-overlapping power-of-two groups. High tier runs bucket groups `{0,1}`, `{2,3}`, etc.; low/debt/AUP keeps one bucket per frame.
Rejected Alternatives: A sliding active-window check was rejected because adjacent frames would repeat half the work and corrupt frame pacing estimates.
Scalability potential: Low stays at 128 one-bucket frames; Middle keeps 64 one-bucket frames when under debt; High/Ultra run two clean buckets per frame with deterministic no-overlap exposure.
Hardware Impact: Estimated 50-300 us duplicate-work avoidance under future registered slow systems, with exact profiler capture still blocked by external compile walls.

## Decision 10: Remove Slow-Accumulator Aliasing For Bucketed Systems
Problem: `IBucketedSlowTickable` objects registered in dispatcher slow lanes were sampled only on the 0.1s slow accumulator, so active bucket IDs could alias against the sample frame and starve or clump future systems.
Solution: Add a dedicated per-frame bucketed slow pass guarded by `_bucketedSlowTickableCount <= 0`; normal slow ticks now skip `IBucketedSlowTickable` objects entirely.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping bucket checks inside `RunSlowTick` was rejected because it looks correct in small tests while failing at frame-rate/cadence gcd boundaries.
Scalability potential: Low pays zero extra work when no bucketed slow systems are registered; High/Ultra can register future bucketed services without sampling artifacts.
Hardware Impact: 0 us hot overhead when count is zero except one integer branch. With future bucketed systems, expected gain is spike removal rather than total work reduction.

Solution: Re-run targeted validation for bucketer-owned files, record the exact current console wall, and avoid patching incomplete memory-defrag work from this bucketer prompt.
Rejected Alternatives: Adding local stubs or forcing `Hecton8.Core.Memory` to reference root `Hecton8.Core` was rejected because it risks circular asmdef damage and would mask another agent's incomplete architecture.
Scalability potential: Bucketer remains isolated and deterministic while the memory-defrag owner repairs their dependency boundary.

## Decision 12: Mirror Registry Service Instead Of Trusting Cached Bucketer
Problem: Dispatcher and voxel integrations could keep a stale bucketer pointer after bootstrap teardown or registry service replacement, causing unsliced work or a disposed service reference.
Solution: Dispatcher now mirrors `GlobalRegistry.SimulationBucketer` every simulation frame, and voxel reacquires when the cached service is null or uninitialized. Bootstrap also initializes an externally registered bucketer if it exists without native storage.
Rejected Alternatives: Hot-swap listener registration was rejected for this pass because a single static registry read is cheaper, simpler, and avoids adding another listener lifecycle path to a central frame authority.
Scalability potential: Low/MX350 retains the 128-bucket flattening after scene transitions; High/Ultra retain two-bucket grouped cadence after service replacement.
Hardware Impact: Dispatcher pays one static service read per frame, estimated below 0.1 us. Avoided fallback queue clumps remain worth 100-600 us on voxel-heavy frames.

## Decision 13: Clamp Entity Bucket Capacity Before Power-Of-Two Rounding
Problem: External callers can pass pathological entity capacity values; unchecked round-up can overflow or request a massive persistent native allocation.
Solution: Add `SimulationBucketConstants.MaxEntityCapacity = 1 << 20` and clamp `ModuloSimulationBucketer.Initialize` before power-of-two rounding. The public helper also guards values above `0x40000000`.
Rejected Alternatives: Trusting bootstrap-only default capacity was rejected because the service contract is public and other agents can call it directly.
Scalability potential: Low devices stay at 8192 by default; High/Ultra can safely scale up to 1,048,576 bucket entries (4 MiB) without allocator surprise.
Hardware Impact: 0 us hot-path cost. Cold initialization avoids accidental multi-GB allocation attempts and catastrophic editor/runtime stalls.

## Cinematic Cheats Used
- Modulo time-slicing fakes continuous slow simulation with staggered authority buckets.
- Thermal diffusion uses 1/8 Jacobi grid slices instead of full-grid physical diffusion per cold tick.
- Biolum distant LOD uses a fast-bucket scheduling fake instead of honest per-frame distance-update cadence.
- Voxel queue ingress uses deterministic fast-bucket deferral instead of immediate physical queue drain.
- AUP safety uses single-bucket cadence throttling instead of recomputing every staggered entity on shift frames.

# Rationale_HEADLESS_SIMULATION_RUNNER

Status: PENDING UNITY RUNTIME VERIFICATION / QA SCOPED-COMPILE CLEAN / GLOBAL EXTERNAL WALLS OUTSIDE DOMAIN

## Decision 0: Disk Memory Bootstrap

Problem: The headless QA assignment requires persistent state before implementation and the required files were absent.
Solution: Create status and rationale files before code work so context compression does not erase assignment state.
Rejected Alternatives: Chat-only tracking is rejected by batch protocol and cannot survive agent handoff.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra tiers unaffected; this is process infrastructure.
Hardware Impact: 0 runtime cost on i3/MX350. No player build path touched.

## Decision 1: Headless QA Boundary

Problem: The prompt targets CI/CD pipeline work, but the runner must inspect ecology, gas, memory, signals, and AUP without owning those domains.
Solution: Add a QA-owned headless assembly that consumes GlobalRegistry interfaces and GlobalSignals lanes, with only small contract additions where no audit surface exists.
Rejected Alternatives: Direct references to concrete gameplay managers in the simulation loop were rejected because 20+ agents are editing in parallel and registry/event surfaces are the sanctioned coupling points.
Scalability potential: Low uses the same audit route with minimal graphics/audio/UI disabled; Middle/High/Ultra can keep richer ecology/gas math alive while the runner remains unchanged.
Hardware Impact: Low-end i3/MX350 avoids rendering/audio/UI bootstrap work; expected gain is dominated by disabled presentation services, runner hot path remains sub-0.1 ms by design.

## Decision 2: Evidence Filter

Problem: QA output can become fake if logs are described as verified before compile/runtime proof exists.
Solution: Mark checklist work as PENDING VERIFICATION until compile and editor/player evidence are captured; use status file as the durable evidence ledger.
Rejected Alternatives: Chat-only success claims and optimistic estimates are rejected by the QA mandate.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra unaffected; this controls reporting quality.
Hardware Impact: 0 runtime impact.

## Decision 3: Crash Signal Lane

Problem: The prompt requires CrashTelemetrySignal consumption, but GlobalSignals only had TelemetryAnomalySignal and ProgressionEventSignal lanes.
Solution: Add a 32-byte CrashTelemetrySignal NativeQueue lane with writer, publish, dequeue, validation, and disposal parity with existing signal lanes.
Rejected Alternatives: Reading CrashTelemetryBuffer directly was rejected because it would couple QA to a concrete runtime owner instead of the signal bus.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra all use the same 32-byte event packet; high-end can produce more postmortem detail through flags without changing queue layout.
Hardware Impact: 64 queued packets at 32 bytes is about 2 KB persistent native memory; MX350/i3 impact is negligible.

## Decision 4: Headless Boot Silence

Problem: Headless CI cannot pay for presentation systems or audio while running a math soak.
Solution: Recognize -h8headless in GameBootstrapper and bypass presentation prewarm plus RenderDispatcher, SpatialAudioManager, ConnectionSplineBatchRenderer, and DebrisManager initialization.
Rejected Alternatives: Initialize-and-disable was rejected because it still allocates GameObjects, render buffers, audio services, and log noise before the runner starts.
Scalability potential: Low tier gets the biggest win by skipping presentation bootstrap; High/Ultra spend saved cycles on actual ecology/gas math instead of invisible rendering.
Hardware Impact: On i3/MX350 the gain is expected to be milliseconds per frame during bootstrap/runtime because graphics/audio/UI work is not created.

## Decision 5: 100x Time Dilation

Problem: Normal gameplay dilation is clamped to 4x, but the assignment requires 100x for CI headless simulation.
Solution: Add RequestHeadlessTimeDilation with a separate 100x clamp and have the runner call it once after dispatcher registration.
Rejected Alternatives: Raising the normal TimeDilationMaximumScalar was rejected because it would let gameplay systems accidentally enter 100x outside QA.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra share the same time source; High/Ultra can absorb the larger workload while Low remains protected by headless presentation bypass.
Hardware Impact: Cold scalar write only; no measurable per-frame overhead beyond the systems intentionally simulating faster.

## Decision 6: Ghost Player AUP

Problem: CI needs chunk/ecology/AUP movement pressure without spawning the player prefab or UI/camera stack.
Solution: Use a Burst IJob over NativeArray<GhostState> to integrate 3D noise movement in AUP space and swap in LateFrame; publish AUP shift signals at 5000m grid crossings.
Rejected Alternatives: Driving HectonPlayerMovement was rejected because it would initialize player, camera, input, UI, and animation dependencies.
Scalability potential: Low uses the same cheap mathematical ghost; High/Ultra can keep expensive downstream ecosystem/gas math active while the ghost cost stays bounded.
Hardware Impact: Estimated <20 us/job on i3/MX350; no managed hot-loop allocations by code inspection.

## Decision 7: Metrics And Exit Discipline

Problem: Long-run QA must fail deterministically on leaks, gas invalidity, predator extinction, or NaN, and must leave evidence before quit.
Solution: Write daily CSV through a preallocated byte-buffer FileStream, track 10-day H8Memory/NativeMemory growth, check gas pressure arrays, and dump a 300-frame NativeArray blackbox before Application.Quit.
Rejected Alternatives: Debug.Log telemetry and post-exit cleanup were rejected; logs can flood CI and post-exit work is not reliable.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra use identical CSV/result/blackbox evidence; top-tier can run longer or with shorter day seconds via args.

## Decision 17: Awaitable Startup Guard

Problem: The runner used `async void Start()`, which can hide exceptions and continue after object teardown if the awaited dispatcher wait resumes late.
Solution: Convert lifecycle entry to `void Start()` and launch `RunStartupAsync(destroyCancellationToken)`. The async body owns its `try/catch`, catches cancellation without failure output, and passes the token into `WaitForDispatcherAndStart`.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping `async void` was rejected by project async policy. Adding `Update()` polling was rejected because the runner already has a cold `Awaitable` path and gameplay-style Update loops are forbidden.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle/High/Ultra behavior is unchanged while active. The gain is failure containment: cancelled startup no longer leaves a late continuation trying to register into dead editor/player state.
Hardware Impact: 0 us in `FastTick`, `FrostTick`, and `LateFrameTick` on i3/MX350. One cold Awaitable startup continuation remains.

## Decision 18: Deferred Ghost Buffer Disposal

Problem: `OnDestroy` completed the pending ghost job before disposing native arrays. That is safe for correctness but creates an avoidable teardown sync point.
Solution: If the ghost job is pending, unregister the two job-owned ghost arrays from `NativeMemorySentinel` and dispose them through `NativeArray.Dispose(JobHandle)`. Non-job-owned blackbox/memory arrays still dispose immediately.
Rejected Alternatives: Blind immediate disposal was rejected as use-after-free risk. Completing the job just to dispose was rejected because the job scheduler can own the disposal dependency directly.
Scalability potential: Low avoids a teardown stall on weak CPUs. High/Ultra gain nothing visually from a blocking teardown sync, so the saved sync budget stays available for actual simulation/visual work in chained runs.
Hardware Impact: 0 us steady-state frame cost. Teardown avoids a potential worker-thread wait; exact microseconds are not measured because Unity MCP/profiler is unavailable.

## Decision 19: Stack-Formatted Result Numbers

Problem: Runtime result JSON wrote numeric values through `.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`. The path is cold, but OMEGA polish explicitly rejects avoidable managed string formatting in QA runtime evidence code.
Solution: Replace numeric result writes with overloads that use stack `Span<char>` plus `TryFormat`, then write the span directly to `StreamWriter`.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving `.ToString()` because it is cold was rejected; the runtime runner is QA evidence infrastructure and should not carry avoidable managed formatting debt.
Scalability potential: Low devices avoid exit-path garbage during fail-fast CI loops. High/Ultra devices get cleaner evidence code without changing the simulation path.
Hardware Impact: 0 us in frame hot paths. Exit/result writing uses stack buffers only for numeric formatting.

## Decision 10

Solution: Resolve both through `IDataVault.GetBuffer<T>` first and keep the old `H8Memory.Allocate<T>` path only as an explicit fallback when the vault is unavailable.
Rejected Alternatives: Removing fallback would make dispatcher startup depend on registry ordering. Keeping only direct `H8Memory` ownership leaves easy Data Sovereignty wins on the table.
Scalability potential: Low keeps deterministic startup through fallback; Middle/High/Ultra get persistent vault-backed shared buffers that can survive dispatcher restarts.
Hardware Impact: Two cold persistent allocations move to vault ownership when available. Runtime hot-path access remains cached `NativeArray` indexing.

## Decision 11

Problem: Dead relocation code in `GlobalDataVault` still contained a future-use hazard even after non-moving defrag was selected.
Solution: Remove the dormant live block move body and retain telemetry-only fragmentation analysis until alias generations exist.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving unused `UnsafeUtility.MemMove` relocation code invites a future caller to re-enable stale pointer behavior.
Scalability potential: Prevents low-tier corruption under memory pressure and lets high-tier defrag be reintroduced behind a handle-generation contract.
Hardware Impact: Avoids accidental cold relocation spikes; no measured runtime delta.

## Decision 12

Problem: `BinaryBlittableSafeAttribute` lived in a one-file `Hecton8.Core.Memory.Layout` asmdef, but CLI verification through `Hecton8.Core.csproj` could not resolve that generated assembly reference.
Solution: Keep the public namespace/type exactly the same, but define the attribute in `MemoryInquisitor.cs`, which is already compiled by the Core project. Remove the empty layout asmdef and the Core asmdef reference.
Rejected Alternatives: Editing generated `.csproj` would be overwritten; keeping a one-file asmdef preserved verification noise.
Scalability potential: Fewer micro-assemblies in the hot Core verification loop; no runtime behavior change.
Hardware Impact: 0 runtime us.

## Decision 13

Problem: The vault grow path still used allocate-copy-free semantics. That keeps the API convenient but can invalidate existing `NativeArray` views when a buffer grows.
Solution: Allow only in-place growth into a contiguous free right block; otherwise return failure and preserve existing pointer stability.
Rejected Alternatives: Copying to a new arena block is unsafe until aliases have generation checks.
Scalability potential: Low tier gets deterministic pointers under memory pressure; High/Ultra can add relocation later behind explicit handles.
Hardware Impact: Removes cold resize copy spikes; no measured runtime claim.

## Decision 14

Problem: Follow-up audit found the previous relocation-removal claim was not fully true: the old defrag move routine and `Relocatable` descriptor flags were still present in `GlobalDataVault`.
Solution: Delete the live relocation routines, remove vault `Relocatable` flags, keep fragmentation analysis as telemetry-only, and dump `Docs/AgentLogs/Dump_PHI_VOD.bin` on active vault buffer allocation/growth failures.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving dead relocation code would allow a future caller to reintroduce stale `NativeArray` aliases. Marking blocks relocatable while refusing relocation is a false memory contract.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle get stable persistent vault views; High/Ultra can add visual/data overkill later only after handle generations or controlled pause-time rebuilds exist.
Hardware Impact: Prevents cold defrag `MemMove` spikes and stale pointer corruption. No measured frame-time gain claimed.

## Decision 15

Problem: `SystemDispatcher` still pushed `SystemPauseSignal` when the vault reported a massive relocation candidate, but relocation is now deliberately disabled.
Solution: Keep the pressure telemetry and remove the pause signal path plus its unused sequence counter.
Rejected Alternatives: Pausing the simulation for non-executed relocation work would trade determinism for a false recovery path.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle avoid artificial stalls under fragmentation pressure; High/Ultra still receive telemetry needed for a future controlled rebuild pass.
Hardware Impact: Avoids a possible frame-level pause caused by telemetry-only defrag. No measured runtime gain claimed.

## Decision 16

Problem: Concurrent vault edits reintroduced live block movement with a compaction fence and address-shift signal. It was safer than the earlier move path, but outstanding `NativeArray` views still do not have a generation-checked handle contract.
Solution: Preserve the newer alignment audit, external-view marking, and telemetry fields, but remove live movement and `Relocatable` block descriptors again.
Rejected Alternatives: Accepting relocation because it emits a signal would still leave unmanaged aliases able to read stale memory.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle keep stable vault views; High/Ultra can re-enable relocation only after all consumers resolve through generation-checked handles or a pause-time rebuild.
Hardware Impact: Avoids possible cold `MemMove` spikes and stale-pointer faults. No measured runtime gain claimed.

## Decision 17

Problem: A final world-streaming verification pass found the relocation body reintroduced again in `GlobalDataVault`, including move/watchdog flags and stale `System.Diagnostics` usage.
Solution: Remove `TryMoveOneBlock`, `MoveOccupiedBlockIntoFreeGap`, stale move/watchdog/pinned flags, `_defragCursor`, and `Relocatable` descriptor emission. Keep macro payload `UnsafeUtility.MemMove` because it copies caller payload bytes into vault-owned cache memory and does not relocate live vault buffers.
Rejected Alternatives: Leaving the method dormant was rejected because previous concurrent passes already proved dormant relocation code gets re-enabled. Removing all `MemMove` calls was rejected because the macro payload copy is not an alias-invalidating relocation path.
Scalability potential: Low/Middle get stable persistent vault views under fragmentation pressure. High/Ultra still have fragmentation telemetry and pending-massive-move signals for a future handle-generation rebuild pass.
Hardware Impact: Prevents cold block-copy spikes and stale unmanaged aliases. Filtered CLI build output is clean for `GlobalDataVault.cs`; no measured frame-time claim.

## Decision 18

Problem: The live relocation block reappeared again during WORLD verification, including stale `_defragCursor` reset lines and move/watchdog constants after the earlier purge.
Solution: Repeat the purge and verify by static scan that the vault has no relocation method, no relocatable descriptor flag, no defrag move cursor, and no stopwatch-based move watchdog.
Rejected Alternatives: Keeping compatibility fields was rejected because they silently invite reactivation and make the status file lie about relocation being removed.
Scalability potential: All tiers keep stable vault addresses. Future high-tier compaction must be implemented as a handle-generation rebuild, not raw block movement.
Hardware Impact: No measured frame-time gain. Prevents cold relocation spikes and alias corruption under fragmentation pressure.
